cards.definitions: A Boolean function family is f=(fₙ:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1})_{n≥1}. A linear decision list consists of s ordered pairs (qᵢ,bᵢ) and a default bit b_{s+1}. On input x, it returns bᵢ at the first i for which qᵢ(x)=1, or the default if all tests fail. Each query is qᵢ(x)=1 iff wᵢ,₀+∑_{j=1}^n wᵢ,ⱼxⱼ>0, with integer weights wᵢ,ⱼ, including the offset wᵢ,₀. Allowing a test for qᵢ(x)=0 is equivalent on integer-valued sums to another query of this form. Size is the number s of queries; weights’ bit lengths are not charged as extra queries. LDL consists of all families admitting, for some fixed constants c,C>0, lists of size at most C(n+1)^c at every n, with no bound on integer weights. LDL_polywt requires in addition constants b,B>0 such that every weight in every list has absolute value at most B(n+1)^b. Constants are uniform across input lengths and queries, but may depend on the family. Neither class requires an algorithm generating the lists. Polynomial magnitude is stronger than polynomial bit length: a weight 2ⁿ has n+1 bits but is not polynomially bounded in magnitude. There is no additional bound on the number of changes in the output sequence (b₁,…,b_{s+1}); it may grow as large as the list length. Proper inclusion means that some family lies in LDL but not LDL_polywt. Equivalently, for that family, every pair of fixed polynomial size and weight bounds fails at some input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some family has polynomial-size unrestricted-weight lists but has no family of polynomial-size, polynomial-magnitude-weight lists, or prove LDL_polywt=LDL by establishing such bounded-weight representations for every LDL family. A lower bound that applies only while alternation depth is restricted does not settle this target.

cards.definitions: For bits s,x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,1}, FANOUTₙ|s,x₁,…,xₙ⟩=|s,s⊕x₁,…,s⊕xₙ⟩, extended linearly to all states; ⊕ is addition modulo two. A permitted circuit acts on n+1+a(n) qubits for some finite a(n)≥0. Its gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitary matrices over ℂ and generalized Toffoli gates: for any k≥1 distinct controls and a distinct target, |z₁,…,z_k,t⟩ maps to |z₁,…,z_k,t⊕(z₁⋯z_k)⟩. Each layer contains gates on disjoint sets of qubits, and depth is the number of layers. Gates may connect any qubits; fanout gates, measurements, postselection and classical feed-forward are not additional primitives. Exact implementation means that for some global phase e^(iφₙ), independent of the input state ψ, Cₙ(|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩^⊗a(n))=e^(iφₙ)(FANOUTₙ|ψ⟩)⊗|0⟩^⊗a(n) for every unit vector ψ in (ℂ²)^⊗(n+1). The ancillas must return to zero, as in the source’s implementation definition. Gate count, ancilla count and gate arities may grow arbitrarily with n but must be finite at each n. The family is nonuniform: there is no required circuit-generation algorithm or finite gate alphabet. The one depth bound d must work for all n. QAC0 usually adds a polynomial-size bound; this question explicitly drops it.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an exact clean-ancilla implementation with a depth bound independent of n, or prove that no such bound exists even when size, ancilla count and Toffoli arity are unrestricted. An approximation with arbitrarily small nonzero error, a lower bound only for polynomial-size circuits, or a bound for one fixed small depth does not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: Fanout is a coherent controlled operation

context_blocks.title: This operation does not clone an arbitrary quantum state
context_blocks.text: For example, applying two-target fanout to |+⟩|00⟩ yields (|000⟩+|111⟩)/√2. It does not yield three independent copies of |+⟩. The target is therefore compatible with the distinction between coherent basis fanout and cloning.

context_blocks.title: Only depth is restricted

The question permits enormous circuits and arbitrarily many zero-initialized ancillas. A negative answer would therefore be a structural limitation of constant depth, beyond ordinary polynomial-size lower bounds.

cards.title: The online Boolean matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The truly subcubic Boolean online problem remains open; structured-matrix and different-product results require separate assumptions.

context_blocks.text: If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.

cards.definitions: A digraph D=(V,A) has labeled vertex set V={1,…,n}, no loops, and at most one arc in each direction between distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Its binary encoding explicitly lists vertices and arcs. A directed cycle has at least two distinct vertices v₁,…,v_ℓ and arcs vᵢ→vᵢ₊₁, with indices modulo ℓ. A k-dicoloring is a map c:V→{1,…,k} such that each color class induces an acyclic digraph, equivalently no directed cycle is monochromatic. The dichromatic number is the least k admitting such a map. The promise problem for k accepts inputs with dichromatic number at most 2 and rejects those with dichromatic number greater than k; inputs with values 3,…,k are outside the promise. The NP-hardness claim means that for each fixed k there is a deterministic algorithm R_k and constants c_k,C_k such that, on a 3-CNF formula F of bit length N, R_k outputs a digraph in time at most C_k(N+1)^c_k, with satisfiable F mapped to the accepting side and unsatisfiable F mapped to the rejecting side. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless P=NP, since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated NP-hardness for every fixed k≥4, or refute that universal hardness assertion. A polynomial-time k-coloring algorithm for some fixed k would contradict the claim under P≠NP. Hardness for k=3, bounds for a growing number of colors, or hardness without the two-colorability completeness promise do not suffice.

cards.title: Can exact fully dynamic APSP have edge-linear amortized updates and polylogarithmic queries?
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

cards.definitions: For each n≥2, X={x₁,…,xₙ} and Y={y₁,…,yₙ} are disjoint alphabets of formal noncommuting variables. A noncommutative polynomial over F is a finite F-linear combination of words in those symbols; multiplication concatenates words and extends bilinearly, so variable order is part of a monomial. Pal_{n,n} has 2n variables, degree 2n and coefficients zero or one. A circuit is a finite acyclic graph whose leaves are variables or arbitrary constants from F and whose internal nodes are binary addition or binary multiplication gates. Multiplication inputs have a designated order. There is one output, fan-out is unrestricted, and the circuit must compute the formal polynomial exactly. Its size is the total number of nodes, as in the original paper. Division gates are not allowed; subtraction is available through the field constant −1. There is no bound on depth, intermediate polynomial degree, coefficient size or circuit uniformity. The syntactic degree of a variable leaf is one and of a constant leaf zero; an addition gate takes the maximum of its children’s syntactic degrees and a multiplication gate takes their sum. The circuit’s syntactic degree is their maximum over all nodes. A polynomial is homogeneous when every nonzero monomial has the same degree; the circuit need not have homogeneous intermediate outputs. The asymptotic claim means: for every fixed field F and every K>0, there is n₀(F,K) such that all n≥n₀ and all circuits computing Pal_{n,n} have more than Kn log₂n nodes. Explicitness is supplied by the displayed polynomial: a word’s coefficient is determined by checking its length, the two alphabets, and the reversed index sequence in time polynomial in n and the word length.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed unrestricted-circuit lower bound beyond every constant multiple of n log n. Bounds only for formulas, homogeneous circuits or restricted syntactic degrees do not suffice. The accepted Raz theorem already proves this claim; a matching quadratic lower bound is stronger than the threshold originally asked for.

context_blocks.title: How the theorem matches the palindrome target
context_blocks.text: Identifying yᵢ with xᵢ turns the polynomial into a one-alphabet palindrome of degree 2n. Its matrix of coefficients indexed by length-n prefixes and suffixes is a permutation matrix: a word occurs exactly when the suffix reverses the prefix. The matrix is full rank over every field, so Raz’s Theorem 1 supplies Ω((2n)√n) product gates. Variable identification cannot increase circuit size; hence this also lower-bounds circuits for the original two-alphabet polynomial.

Raz’s accepted result gives Ω(n^(3/2)) for an explicit degree-proportional family and also applies to the palindrome target after identifying corresponding x and y variables. No extra restriction on the original circuit is needed.

Identifying yᵢ with xᵢ turns the polynomial into a one-alphabet palindrome of degree 2n. Its matrix of coefficients indexed by length-n prefixes and suffixes is a permutation matrix: a word occurs exactly when the suffix reverses the prefix. The matrix is full rank over every field, so Raz’s Theorem 1 supplies Ω((2n)√n) product gates. Variable identification cannot increase circuit size; hence this also lower-bounds circuits for the original two-alphabet polynomial.

Shastri’s revised May preprint states a tight Ω(nd) bound for Pal_{n,d}, giving Ω(n²) when d=n. The card’s resolved n log n threshold does not depend on independently accepting that stronger proof: the accepted Raz result already crosses the required threshold.

cards.definitions: An input consists of integers d≥r≥1, a rational d×r matrix B with linearly independent columns, and a positive rational threshold R. All rationals are given by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators with delimiters; N is the total bit length. The lattice is L(B)={Bz:z∈ℤ^r}⊆ℝ^d. For fixed p∈[1,2], the norm is ‖x‖_p=(∑_{i=1}^d|xᵢ|^p)^(1/p), and λ₁^(p)(L)=min{‖v‖_p:v∈L, v≠0}. SVP_{p,γ} accepts if λ₁^(p)(L)≤R and rejects if λ₁^(p)(L)>γR. Inputs between these thresholds are outside the promise; either answer is permitted there. The requested task is gap decision, not output of a lattice vector. The norm parameter and gap are fixed mathematical constants, not part of the input, and one finite deterministic Turing-machine program must solve all promised inputs for them. A subexponential bound means time at most 2^{h(d)}N^c for some fixed c and nonnegative h with h(d)/d→0. Bounds and programs may depend on p and γ. The dimension convention follows the source’s lower-bound statements for lattices in ℝ^d; rank r≤d is displayed separately. ETH here asserts that for some δ>0 there is no deterministic algorithm deciding 3-CNF satisfiability on v variables in O(2^{δv}M^c) time for any fixed c, where M is the formula’s bit length. It is the ordinary satisfiability assumption, not a promise that unsatisfiable instances have a constant fraction of violated clauses. Randomized ETH instead excludes bounded-error randomized algorithms and is a different premise. The card follows the literal deterministic-ETH version of Open Problem 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the implication from ordinary deterministic ETH to the stated constant-gap subexponential lower bound for every fixed p∈[1,2]. The constant γ may depend on p but must be strictly greater than one and independent of dimension. A result using GapETH, or only randomized ETH, does not by itself prove this precise implication.

cards.title: Sample stretching and the meaning of independent synthetic observations
cards.formal: Given k independent observations from an unknown discrete distribution p on a domain Ω, what is the smallest distortion ε for which an algorithm can output k+1 independent observations from a distribution p′ with dTV(p,p′)≤ε? The intended dependence of p′ on the input data, the independence convention and the accuracy guarantee remain to be specified.
cards.why: Investigates what genuinely new statistical information can be supplied from a fixed dataset. Independence is central: synthetic observations can have plausible marginals while substantially overstating the effective amount of data.

cards.definitions: A discrete probability distribution p on a finite or countable set Ω assigns nonnegative masses p(x) summing to one. Total variation is dTV(p,q)=(1/2)∑_{x∈Ω}|p(x)−q(x)|. The k input observations X₁,…,X_k have joint law p^⊗k, meaning Pr[X₁=x₁,…,X_k=x_k]=∏ᵢp(xᵢ). A sample transformation sees only these observations, the known domain and k, and may use private randomness independent of the input. It has no further sampling access to p. One possible literal output requirement is: for every p there exists a fixed q_p with Law(Y₁,…,Y_{k+1})=q_p^⊗(k+1) and dTV(p,q_p)≤ε, where the law averages over both input samples and private randomness. A different requirement allows a random distribution Q inferred from the data and asks for conditionally iid outputs given Q, together with a specified probabilistic accuracy guarantee for dTV(p,Q). The latter generally gives a mixture of product laws after averaging over Q, not a product law. Yet another condition, used in sample amplification, is dTV(Law(Y₁,…,Y_{k+1}),p^⊗(k+1))≤ε. Here distance is on Ω^(k+1), whereas the original source compares distributions on Ω. These three formulations must not be identified. For a finite domain Ω={1,…,n}, any resulting optimal distortion would be a function of k and n; the source also allows a general discrete domain.
cards.answer_criterion: After fixing the source’s intended output and accuracy conventions and the domain class, determine the optimal distortion as a function of the parameters, with matching attainable upper and universal lower bounds, or with a proved infimum if attainment is not required. Results for a different joint-output or conditional-independence guarantee do not settle the chosen target.
